tagline: Mill towns, working forests and mountain views between Baxter’s entrances
intro: The wider Katahdin Woods & Waters National Scenic Byway runs 89 miles between Baxter State Park’s entrances, through farms, meadows and working forests. It passes between Ambajejus and Millinocket lakes and follows the Penobscot River toward Patten. The National Scenic Byway Foundation records its 2021 national designation for recreation, highlighting canoeing, hiking, fishing and other outdoor pursuits. The northern end reaches the East Branch’s headwaters and Grand Lake Matagamon; farther south, the historic mill towns provide museums, galleries and information about the region’s lumber industry.

Road transport changed the region’s timber trade in 1971, when environmental concerns ended river transport of pulpwood and Great Northern opened the Golden Road to its Millinocket mill. That private road parallels the West Branch. A different land legacy frames the scenic journey: Governor Percival Baxter bought more than 200,000 acres with his own money and gave them to Maine on condition that they remain “forever wild.”

Traveling from the northern entrance at Grand Lake Matagamon, the wider byway reaches Patten before continuing toward Millinocket. Ash Hill lies just south of Patten, with a view of Katahdin. The route includes Stacyville, Medway and East Millinocket, then Millinocket and the lakes before reaching Baxter’s southern entrance.

moments.title: Patten
moments.text: Patten’s Lumbermen’s Museum devotes nine buildings to the work and equipment of the woods. Its subjects include river drivers, remote logging camps and the bateaux used to carry supplies by water. The collection covers the 1800s and the first three decades of the 1900s, including the Lombard Steam Hauler and Peavey Cant Dog. Lumbering also shaped the town’s farms and commerce: Patten became a distribution center serving the surrounding timber country. Fish Stream once carried local timber downstream toward mills at Old Town and Bangor, linking the town’s cutting grounds with markets farther south.

moments.title: Ash Hill
moments.text: Ash Hill, just south of Patten, offers a 360-degree view of Katahdin and the mountains surrounding Baxter State Park. The view extends toward the Allagash and Aroostook County. Katahdin is Maine’s highest mountain and the northern end of the Appalachian Trail.
moments.notice: Look toward Katahdin and the surrounding Baxter mountains, with longer views toward the Allagash and Aroostook County.

moments.title: Millinocket
moments.text: A paper mill required a new town at Millinocket. Construction of Great Northern’s mill began in May 1899, after engineer Charles W. Mullen proposed using the Penobscot’s water power. Italian stonemasons carried much of the construction work; their contracted passage to the United States left them in debt when they arrived. The town incorporated in 1901. Its economy centered on forest products and recreation, and the paper company closed in 2008. The Bangor and Aroostook Railroad had arrived in 1894, opening the area to development before the mill builders began their work.
